text: You now know how to build account and subscription boundaries on both clouds. Neither Azure nor AWS tells you where those boundaries should actually go, and the default answer most teams reach for — mirror the org chart — is the single most common multi-account design mistake. This lesson is the framework that replaces it.

An org chart describes who reports to whom, not what should fail together. One subscription per team gets redrawn every time people move between teams, and it's usually the wrong size in both directions at once — too coarse to separate a team's risky production database from its low-stakes internal wiki, too fine to let a security boundary span the teams that actually need to share one. The question to ask instead is blast radius: if this one account or subscription were fully compromised, misconfigured, or hit a hard limit, what's the worst case? That worst case is the boundary.

Four dimensions tend to decide where a real boundary belongs, and they don't always agree. Security blast radius contains a compromised credential to where it started — production versus non-production is the line almost every design draws first. Compliance scope keeps a regulated workload's audit boundary small instead of pulling the whole company into one audit. Billing isolation gives a cost-volatile workload its own dedicated budget. And operational access draws a line around who legitimately needs access, even when the other three don't force one.

Two anti-patterns share the same root cause from opposite directions. One account per team inherits every org-chart problem already covered. One shared account for everything ignores blast radius just as badly, the other way — a single mistake anywhere in that account has a blast radius equal to the entire company's cloud footprint.

Whatever framework an organization settles on becomes the actual decision logic inside the subscription vending pipeline or the Account Factory request from the last two lessons — workload type, data sensitivity, and cost profile determine which management group or OU a new boundary lands in automatically, closing out this chapter's answer to where landing zone boundaries actually belong.
